newsitem.title: USA: Republicans celebrate $11 million in fund raising.
newsitem.headline: Republicans celebrate $11 million in fund raising.

text.p: The Republican party Tuesday night celebrated an $11 million fund raising coup in the midst of unprecedented scrutiny into the way politicians raise money.

Elegantly dressed men and women were met by protesters demanding finance reform and shouting "$5,000 a plate, Americans can't afford this date" as they entered a Washignton hotel for the party's biggest annual fund raising event.

The elected officials, lobbyists and political professionals largely ignored the shouting and spent the evening revelling in the success of a party that now controls both houses of Congress and a majority of the country's governorships.
But the issue of who gives what and what they get for it that has dogged both major parties for most of the past year crept into the ballroom nonetheless.

The party, said New Jersey Gov. Christine Todd Whitman, places a price on the spirit of founder Abraham Lincoln -- "not a price on his bedroom." The reference was to the Democratic party's perks for favoured insiders that have included stays in Lincoln's bedroom in President Clinton's White House.
Party chairman Jim Nicholson said Democrats have "yet to return money they took from drug smugglers ... and Chinese Communists."

The Democrats have acknowledged receiving more than $3 million in questionable foreign funds last year and were in the process of returning them. Last week the Republican National Committee said it had returned more than $100,000 in political contributions because it learned the money came from the Hong Kong parent company of a U.S. subsidiary.

Organisers said Tuesday's event was the culmination of nearly four months of fund raising that raked in more than $11 million for the GOP treasury. Ted Welch, who chaired the event, told the crowd as they sat down to salmon and filet mignon that a recent Democratic effort raised only $4 million -- "so we have a lot to cheer for."
CNN reported Tuesday that because of the spotlight that fund raising has come under the Democrats have collected less than half of the $4 million pledged two weeks ago.

Public Citizen, the "public interest" lobbying group that organised the protest outside the GOP event, fielded 20 to 30 protesters who were noiser than their numbers. They included a man dressed as a cigar-chomping black cat -- symbolic of the "fat cat" contributors at whom the protest was aimed.
He rode the streets around the hotel sitting in the back seat of a convertible holding white money bags in both hands.
"Corruption, bribery ... democracy for sale," shouted a man into a bullhorn at a hearby corner as cars and buses passed with party goers.

The protest was designed to back a drive by Common Cause to collect 1.776 million signatures on a petition asking Congress to pass campaign finance reform legislation. Bob Schiff, an organiser of the protest, said about a quarter of a million such signatures have been collected.
Nor was he dismayed that Sen. John McCain, R-Ariz., the leading GOP backer of campaign finance reform in the Senate, was on the guest list for Tuesday'e event.
"He definitely wants the system changed," he said. "Maybe he'll be able to do something about it from inside the party."
